question.leadin: This policy was enforced by the Volstead Act.
question.text: Name this policy, which banned the sale or prodution of alcoholic beverages in the United States between 1920 and 1933.
question.clue: A hatchet was used in activism for this policy by Carrie Nation.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about odd presidential pets.
swap.text: This president owned a pet raccoon named Rebecca. This former Massachusetts governor famously said "You lose" to a woman who tried to win a bet by getting him to say more than two words.
swap.clue: The Bonus Act was passed despite this president's veto.

question.leadin: A letter written to this man in 1934 proclaims "Even if my business hasn't been strictly legal, it don't hurt anything to tell you what a fine car you got in the V-8."
question.text: Name this American industrialist whose company introduced its first V-8 car in 1932, five years after it discontinued its landmark Model T.
question.clue: This businessman used the scientific management ideas of Frederick W. Taylor to improve efficiency on each of the eighty-four steps of his signature product.

swap.leadin: In 1920, this man ran for US President from a prison cell after being arrested for sedition.
swap.text: Name this politician who, with "Big Bill" Haywood, helped found the Industrial Workers of the World.
swap.clue: While participating in the ARU, this man was arrested for interfering with the mail, and was later represented by Clarence Darrow.

question.leadin: The plaintiff in this case appealed his violation of the Bakeshop Act of 1895, which stated that bakery employees could only work 60 hours a week.
question.text: Name this progressive-era case, which upheld the "liberty of contract" in ruling against limiting the hours that bakers could work.
question.answerHtml: Lochner v. New York [or New York v. Lochner]
question.clue: The argument that the Fourteenth Amendment does not "enact" Spencer's Social Statics was put forth in Holmes's dissent.

swap.text: In 1904, this muckraking journalist wrote The History of Standard Oil Company, detailing the company's abusive practices as part of a series of articles for McClure's Magazine.
swap.clue: This woman who described J.D Rockefeller's manipulation of railroad rates in The History of the Standard Oil Company.

question.leadin: The Spooner Act authorized the purchase of a company that was involved in this project.
question.text: Name this project that was the subject of the Hay-Herran and Hay-Bunau-Varilla treaties. Major challenges during this project included making the Culebra Cut and treating workers suffering from malaria and yellow fever.
question.clue: The building of this structure was made possible by Walter Reed's work controlling Yellow Fever.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about "Robber Baron" industrialists.
swap.text: J.P. Morgan and other industrialists helped save the economy during this economic panic, which saw the collapse of the Knickerbocker Trust Company.
swap.clue: This crisis occurred after an attempt by Otto and Augustus Heinze to corner the United Copper Company.

question.leadin: Name these "amendments" governing the Latin American policy of the U.S.
question.text: This law, named for the Connecticut senator who put it forth on behalf of Secretary of State Root, permitted an exclusive U.S. right to intervene in Cuba.
question.clue: This legislation prohibited a certain entity from entering into debt that it could not pay, or from making territorial concessions to anybody except the United States.

swap.leadin: This one-time Governor of New York left his Supreme Court seat to run against Wilson in 1916, only to end up back on the Court years later as Hoover's Chief Justice.
swap.text: Identify this man who presided over the "Sick Chicken Case," Schechter Poultry Co. v. US, as well as West Coast Hotel v. Parrish.
swap.clue: He replaced Bainbridge Colby as Secretary of State and chaired the Washington Naval Conference.

question.leadin: Answer the following about a particular piece of legislation.
question.text: This 1913 legislation lowered the rates from the earlier Payne-Aldrich Tariff and called for a federal income tax.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about a monumental effort.
swap.text: This secretary of state under presidents McKinley and Roosevelt signed a treaty with Lord Pauncefote of Britain granting the U.S. exclusive rights to build the canal. In that position he also formulated the Open Door policy to treat with China.
swap.clue: This man, who got his start as Lincoln's personal secretary, negotiated the treaty to end the war with Spain, and negotiated the treaty to build the Panama Canal. He also established the "Open Door" policy with China.

question.text: This railroad trust that combined the companies of E.H. Harriman and James Hill was targeted by Theodore Roosevelt and declared unconstitutional in a namesake 1904 Supreme Court case.
question.answerHtml: Northern Securities Company [accept Northern Securities Company v. U.S.]
question.clue: Following the bankruptcy of the Northern Pacific Railway, J.P. Morgan formed this company to consolidate Midwestern railroads before it was declared a monopoly in a 1904 Supreme Court case.

swap.text: The racist and revisionist histories Du Bois attacked in Black Reconstruction were exemplified by this author's book Division and Reunion. This president led the United States through World War I.
swap.clue: McReynolds prevented an official photo of the Court from being taken because he refused to sit next to a Jew, namely another one of this President's nominees, Louis Brandeis.

question.text: A bridge between Staten Island and New Jersey is named for this civil engineer who supervised the construction of the canal.
question.clue: This man led the damming of the Chagres River and the building of locks that formed Lake Gatun.

swap.text: This most successful American fighter ace during World War One, was a character witness in Billy Mitchell's court martial. This CEO of Eastern Air Lines visited Russia during World War Two to study the Soviet air force.

question.text: Rankin supported this progressive 1921 act, named for a couple of senators from Texas and Iowa, which provided federal money to states for maternity and child care. It was administered by the Children's Bureau of the Department of Labor.
question.answerHtml: Sheppard-Towner Act [accept the “Promotion of the Welfare and Hygiene of Maternity and Infancy Act”]
question.clue: One Harding bright spot was this act, which funded a system of prenatal and child health clinics in one of the first American welfare programs. It was spearheaded by the first woman to head a federal bureau, Julia Lathrop.

swap.text: After helping to found the IWW and organizing the Paint Creek Strike in Kentucky, this Irish immigrant helped recruit coal miners into the United Mine Workers to prepare for the Ludlow Strikes despite being 83 years old.
swap.answer: Mary Harris Jones or Mother Jones
swap.clue: This union leader unsuccessfully attempted to prevent the strike from turning into an armed action. This figure is better known being an important figure in the Knights of Labor and for leading a "children's crusade," a march on Theodore Roosevelt's home.

question.leadin: She was the first president of the Negro Fellowship League, which provided assistance to black migrants in the north, and her life's work was chronicled in A Red Record and Crusade for Justice.

swap.text: The siege of Veracruz occurred in response to this diplomatic incident named for the oil rich city in Tamaulipas that it occurred in. Like much of history, this event was exacerbated by neither side's ability to overcome their language barrier.
swap.clue: Huerta himself did not last long, as this incident, in which Mexican soldiers temporarily imprisoned some American sailors, gave Woodrow Wilson a pretext for invading Veracruz and ousting Huerta.
